sections.title: The product rule along a path

opening: In Chapters 1 and 2, we modeled computation as a step-by-step sequence of transitions between discrete configurations and showed how any Boolean circuit can be made logically reversible—preserving enough information at every gate to undo the entire calculation and clear temporary workspace through uncomputation. Up to this point, however, our registers have always occupied a single definite bit string at each stage of a run.
opening_continuation: We now take our first step into quantum computation. Between measurements, a quantum register evolves through reversible steps, yet when we observe the register, the outcome can be probabilistic. What mathematical description must replace a single deterministic path through configurations? In this chapter, we first place deterministic, nondeterministic, and probabilistic transitions into a unified framework of weighted state diagrams and time-expanded paths, governed by the product rule along a path and the sum rule across paths. We then show why nonnegative probabilities can never allow two random-looking steps to cancel out into a certain outcome, and we introduce the signed and complex probability amplitudes that make quantum interference possible—culminating in why leftover path information in a workspace register destroys interference unless it is uncomputed.
intro_continuation: Why does the second step undo the randomness of the first instead of compounding it? When a register can reach the same final configuration along two different intermediate paths—passing through 0 or passing through 1—classical probability assigns positive weights to both routes, so opening additional paths to an outcome can only increase its chance of occurring. To explain how two alternative paths to 1 can completely cancel each other out while the paths to 0 reinforce, we must replace probabilities with probability amplitudes—weights that carry signs and phases—and discover how quantum interference reshapes the rules of computation.
